articles.title: LSU just dared the SEC to enforce its own rules. Now the conference has a major problem
articles.summary: After Will Wade played RJ Luis on Wednesday night, the league is at a crossroads. Is Greg Sankey willing to make an example of LSU?
articles.body:
So you say you want conference self-governance. College sports has gotten so out of control under the NCAA banner that the only path forward is to make the rules and enforce the rules, all on your own.

Welcome to the Thunderdome, SEC. When you walk inside, here you find LSU, once again playing by its own rules created by its own Louisiana judges, mocking you to your face and daring you to prove that you have the stomach to enforce rules the rest of the conference wants.

At the most fundamental level, what happened Wednesday night when the LSU men's basketball team put former NBA G League signee RJ Luis on the floor is the first big test of whether conference self-governance even has a chance of working now that the power leagues have tried and failed (thus far) to get the Protect College Sports Act to the finish line in Congress.

Barring a stunning reversal in the direction of the wind on Capitol Hill, the SEC and Big Ten have determined that this is the likely future of their enterprise in the near-term. In order to take back some control over eligibility rules from lawyers and judges, they have largely decided they must do it themselves.

Problem is, this requires good faith and cooperation among a lot of schools who mostly operate as independent entities and answer primarily to their fans and donors, not a conference office or some higher ethical standard about what's appropriate in college sports.

So all it takes is one bad-faith actor to mess everything up. And LSU is, more often than not, willing to push the envelope with Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry at the controls, a figurehead athletic director in Verge Ausberry and a head coach in Will Wade who thinks he's bulletproof after being fired from LSU in 2022 for major NCAA rules violations only to get the job back four years later.

"It's like a scene from 'Dumb and Dumber,'" one longtime SEC administrator told Yahoo Sports.

The restrained and conservative way to frame the reaction when Luis checked in about eight minutes into LSU's 79-67 win over Louisiana-Monroe is that people across the SEC were furious and in some cases bewildered by the audacity of it all.

If you haven't followed this stuff closely enough to understand why, don't worry. It's complicated and mentally exhausting to keep up with every college eligibility mess that ends up in court these days.

But particularly with college basketball, some schools and coaches decided last season that they could add players who had left college years earlier and get them eligible through a temporary-restraining order even if they had been drafted by NBA teams, signed two-way contracts or played in the G League. As you can imagine, the NCAA disagreed.

It also caused a major backlash, particularly within the SEC where former Alabama player Charles Bediako came back three years after turning pro , got a TRO, played five games and then became ineligible again after a different judge denied his request for a preliminary injunction .

In August, the SEC voted for new rules that would allow the conference to suspend coaches who bring back former pros and fine schools 50 percent of their athletic budgets, with commissioner Greg Sankey having wide latitude to impose more penalties. The motivation to pass this rule was — you guessed it — LSU football coach Lane Kiffin trying to bring back players who had left NFL training camps.

Ultimately, after a bunch of strongly worded statements and threats of expelling LSU from the league , LSU backed down and decided not to roster the former pros because they'd be crazy to do anything else. Right? Right?

Well, crazy is apparently back in town in the form of Wade, one of the sport's classic scoundrels (even he would most likely not mind that label) who cares little about his colleagues' affection and even less about, you know, rules. Remember, this is the same guy who was caught on an FBI wiretap detailing how he tried to buy a player before it was allowed , missed the 2019 NCAA tournament because he refused to cooperate with the school's ensuing investigation and then held onto his job three more years until the NCAA's allegations came finally down.

After firing Wade, LSU became really bad at basketball for four years. Empowered by Landry and the president he picked, Wade Rousse, LSU decided the only way to fix that was to bring back Wade, whose reputation had been cleansed by two years at McNeese State (where Rousse had been president previously) and one at NC State. With NCAA rules and judges across the country ushering in the pay-for-play era, Wade's past transgressions no longer mattered. What could go wrong?

Well, since LSU had no players when Wade returned, he unleashed his staff across the world to offer huge sums of money to a variety of players in Europe and former college players who would be willing to learn what the Louisiana legal system might be able to do for them. Enter Luis, who left St. John's in 2025 after being named Big East player of the year, went undrafted, signed a two-way contract with the Utah Jazz and even was part of a trade before his 2025-26 season was shut down due to injury.

LSU signed him, sparking multiple lawsuits in multiple places. The argument in favor of Luis is that, from a fairness standpoint, college basketball is filled with players from Europe who signed with club teams as young teenagers, technically making them just as professional. The argument against is that you have to draw the line somewhere, and if the college part of college basketball matters, you can't give eligibility to someone who willingly left college early to pursue a pro career and then wants to come back because things didn't quite work out.

Both perspectives have some validity. But in general, nearly everyone in college sports — and particularly within the SEC — supports the idea that adding G League players is ridiculous, even if there's a loophole or a TRO that allows it. Everyone except LSU.

This is where the self-governance concept meets the reality of what it will actually look like. By playing Luis — going two steps further than even Kiffin — a line in the sand has been drawn.

LSU is daring the SEC to go beyond strongly worded statements and do something drastic. Suspensions? Fines? A vote to expel them from the league? But then there's the legal implications, which are unclear and potentially unpredictable. In another win for billable hours, everyone is putting their general counsels to work.

The word early Thursday, prior to a meeting of SEC presidents, potentially centered on schools boycotting games against LSU. Particularly in states that aren't Louisiana, the thought is that this might hold up legally.

"I'm ready to take action," one league athletic director told Yahoo Sports. "But trying to cover all bases. These next 36 hours will be interesting."

Indeed, they will — with the concept of conference self-governance either proving to be a potential pathway toward college sports sanity or an idea that gets pronounced dead on arrival.

articles.title: Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards speaks on decision to undergo knee surgery, has no clear return timeline: 'Whenever my knee tells me it's ready, then I'll be ready'
articles.summary: Edwards is set to miss multiple months after undergoing arthroscopic surgery on his ailing right knee on Oct. 27.
articles.body:
Three weeks after undergoing arthroscopic surgery on his ailing knee , Minnesota Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards is speaking out about his recovery.

On Thursday, the guard talked to reporters for the first time since the procedure, saying that the rehabilitation process was "going great" and that he was focused on improving the strength in his leg post-surgery. Edwards also spoke about the timeline of his injury before deciding to go under the knife, saying that his knee had been bothering him on and off for years but that it had "flared up" significantly last month.

"It was frustrating, but I realized I had to do it, so I just made my mind up that same day, like we're gonna do it tomorrow," Edwards said.

The 25-year-old guard said that he had managed his knee well in the offseason and that it was still "good" in camp. But by the Timberwolves' season opener on Oct. 21, it was getting worse, and was "really bothering" him in the team's win over the Orlando Magic on Oct. 23.

Minnesota's back-to-back on Oct. 25 and Oct. 26, against the Toronto Raptors at home and the Cleveland Cavaliers away, is when it really started to be a problem: "After the back-to-back it was really bad, like painful to fly," Edwards said.

Edwards said that he hopes that the surgery will help mitigate the pain going forward.

"It was something that I needed, it needed to be done in order for me to be able to play without any pain for the next couple years," Edwards said. "But who knows, maybe in a couple years I might have to get something else, but hopefully not. I think I'll be pretty good."

Edwards, who said that this is the longest he's ever gone without playing basketball, added that he plans on coming back this season but doesn't have a clear timeline. At the time of his surgery, reports indicated that he would need more than two months to recover.

"I have no clue. Whenever my knee tells me it's ready, then I'll be ready," he said of a return to the court.

Losing Edwards initially seemed to be a brutal blow to the Timberwolves' chances: Before the surgery, Edwards was averaging 33.3 points per game and seemed on track for another dominant season. But Minnesota has fared well in his absence, going 8-3 in the weeks since Edwards' surgery.

"I was thirsty to get back, especially after the first game," Edwards said, referring to the Timberwolves' loss to the Golden State Warriors right after his procedure. "I was ready to get back and just get in their ear, tell them what I'm seeing, feel the energy. But after that game, we kinda took off, so I was like, I'll take my time. But I'm happy to be around now."

While speaking to reporters, Edwards had high praise for all of his teammates, specifically pointing out the "phenomenal" play of Ayo Dosunmu — who currently leads the team in points — and noting that forward Jaden McDaniels is "stepping up big time." He also confirmed that he's been sharing his scouting reports with his teammates, staying involved in the team despite his absence from the court.

Led by Dosunmu and LaMelo Ball, Minnesota is currently fourth in the Western Conference with a 11-4 record and a pretty favorable schedule over the next few weeks.

articles.title: ‘I ain’t no Laker fan’… Kevin Garnett admits Luka Doncic is undeniable and he loves watching him
articles.summary: Former Boston Celtics star Kevin Garnett admits he loves watching Luka Doncic play for the LA Lakers. Luka Doncic is in MVP form this season, leading the LA...
articles.body:
Former Boston Celtics star Kevin Garnett admits he loves watching Luka Doncic play for the LA Lakers.

Luka Doncic is in MVP form this season, leading the LA Lakers to a 13-3 record to start the season. While they lost their most recent game to the Utah Jazz, they remain the #1 seed in the Western Conference.

Doncic is averaging 38.1 points per game this season, along with 7.0 rebounds and 7.6 assists.

NBA legend Kevin Garnett says that while he is no fan of the Lakers, he has to give Doncic credit where it is due.

Speaking to the KG & Stephen A. podcast, Garnett said that he loves how Doncic makes all of the players around him better.

He explained: "[There's] going to be a bunch of stuff we see Luka [Doncic] do that you ain't never seen him do straight up this year.

"I love his game, bro. He has his own pace. He complains a little bit too much for me, but he controls the game the way he controls it, and I feel like he puts guys in positions to where he can make them better."

Garnett says he has enjoyed watching the aggressiveness the Lakers play with, and he cannot help but admire them.

He said of Doncic: "When he's out there, Austin Reaves – he flows and all that, man, it flows, bro. And they got some players that play hard, right? The Lakers, they play hard.

"Now, I ain't no Laker fan or none of that. I'm just [making an] observation, but when he's out there, bro, he's controlling that s***."

The Lakers face the Sacramento Kings next, before getting the chance to make amends for their latest loss when they face the Utah Jazz. That defeat ended a long winning streak.

Then comes the game fans have been waiting for, when the Lakers face the San Antonio Spurs in the NBA Cup, with Victor Wembanyama emerging as Doncic's biggest early rival for the MVP Award.

articles.title: 9 worst contracts in the NBA: Trae Young, Devin Booker headline list of players that are toughest to trade
articles.summary: While no NBA contract is technically "untradeable," these NBA stars will be exceedingly difficult to move.
articles.body:
No NBA contract is untradeable, no matter how bad it is. Just a year ago, Paul George ranked No. 3 on my list of worst contracts in the NBA . The Sixers were able to flip him this summer for Jaylen Brown, helping to vault them to the top of the East this season.

The missing part of that analysis, of course, is that Philadelphia had to attach two first-round picks and two second-rounders in order to move off George's deal. Many of the highest-paid players in the league would need the same treatment if they were to switch teams because of how underwater their contracts are.

It can be tricky to trade some of those good-but-overpaid stars, but it's never impossible. Using my salary model , we can see exactly how bad some of these massive long-term contracts are. Here are the deals that are the toughest to trade right now.

It might surprise some to see Booker as the worst contract in the league. He was an All-Star last season, leading a plucky Suns team to 45 wins. He's having another good scoring year, averaging 25 points per game on solid efficiency. He's only 30 years old, so he should still have plenty more left in the tank.

Booker is a good player. I had him No. 20 in the league in my preseason starter rankings . DARKO, the all-in-one metric that my salary model is built upon, is lower on him. He's right outside the top 50 due to a poor defensive impact. Booker has had periods where he's defended well earlier in his career, but the consistency isn't there anymore on a nightly basis. That kills his value in my model and makes him a much more unattractive trade candidate than you might expect.

Despite Booker's flaws, he's worth a large salary in the $30-$35 million range. The problem is that he will be making double that amount when his contract ends in 2030. He's not close to an MVP candidate, which is the level that he would have to get to in order to justify being one of the top eight highest-paid players throughout his deal. Add in the multiple years remaining on his contract, and he's the most overpaid star in my model.

Young signed a four-year, $212 million contract extension this past summer that was instantly one of the worst in the league the moment that the pen hit the paper. It's not clear exactly who the Wizards were bidding against given the low price they paid to acquire him via trade.

That extension looks even worse given Young's play this season. He's still passing the ball well, but his scoring ability has declined considerably and his sky-high usage has impeded the development of some of the most important players on the team.

Even given that decline, Young is still a quality starter who is worth about $30 million per season. But he's averaging over $50 million in salary through 2030-31. Additionally, he hasn't been able to adapt to playing off the ball, making him a tough fit in many places. There's no clear team that would want him, even if the Wizards were willing to attach the multiple picks that it would take to get off his contract. MORE: What did the NBA and the rest of the sports world look like the last time a GTA game was released?

Embiid has fortunately been able to stay on the floor this year. But his decline has been obvious. He's averaging a career-low 20 points per game and shooting below 40 percent from the field. His 3-point touch has completely evaporated. And while he is suppressing shots at the rim on defense, his mobility and jumping ability aren't there on most nights.

Embiid is still a decent starter, and far better than any other option that the Sixers have at center. But he's the sixth-highest-paid player in the league this season, earning $58 million. And he has two more years remaining on a deal that keeps on going up. Given his rapid decline, injury history and price tag, nobody is going to want to trade for him unless the Sixers give up some first-round picks or trade for another contract on this list.

DARKO has George playing at an All-Star level. His contract is still a negative due to a few reasons: First, he has the 11th-highest salary in the league at $56.6 million. Second, his minutes projection is low due to his health issues in recent years. And third, DARKO has been a bit slow to catch up to his improved play this season.

George has been the second-best player on one of the best teams in the East. His 3-point shooting and defense have been the perfect fit in Boston. But he's still overpaid. If the Celtics tried to move him on his current deal, it would cost less than the two first-rounders that the Sixers paid, but they would still need to attach something. For that reason, he's more valuable to them if he plays rather than gets traded. MORE: How Victor Wembanyama is on pace to shatter the single-season dunk record

Davis is one of the most likely players in the league to get traded. Whoever makes that move must be extremely careful with the contract that they give him.

Davis is seeking a max extension that would pay him $275 million and extend his deal by four years, according to reporting from The Athletic . That would be a disastrous deal given that Davis is already overpaid on his current contract.

Davis is averaging 24.6 points per game this season, but his efficiency is middling for a big man. He's a good rim finisher and is having a surprisingly solid start from 3. He's below average everywhere else on the floor, though. He's one of the highest-volume midrange shooters in the game, where he's hitting only 37 percent of his shots.

Defensively, Davis is still a great rim protector. His transition defense has been abysmal this year, though, dragging his overall impact numbers down. Perhaps that changes in a winning situation, but that's a big bet to make.

Davis' health, decline and contract demands make him a very risky trade candidate. The talent is there, though, as is the availability. Some team will probably take a chance on him and may come to regret it sooner rather than later.

Bridges was a key contributor to the Knicks ' championship team last season, providing good defense, 3-point shooting and shot creation from the midrange. He hasn't looked like the same player, though, this year. His offense has been way down across the board.

That is problematic for the Knicks because Bridges is in the first year of a four-year deal that pays him $150 million. He's been average at best, but he's being paid like a fringe All-Star.

The Knicks used five picks to acquire Bridges a few years ago. That did result in a championship and some big moments from him, but they would need to attach picks to move him now.

Sabonis wants out of Sacramento, according to ESPN's Tim MacMahon . The problem is that there is no team interested in his services.

Sabonis is a tough fit because, in order to maximize his All-Star talent, the ball needs to go through him. His defensive shortcomings also make it tough to build a contending team with him playing center.

Sabonis has another season left on his deal after this one, and he's making close to $50 million next season. He's still an elite rebounder, but his scoring is way down this season. A rebuilding team could use him as an overpaid floor-raiser, but nobody is giving up anything of value to obtain him.

The Spurs would be very wise to move off Fox's deal soon. They already have a crowded guard rotation that has necessitated starting Fox alongside Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper. That could become untenable once Tobias Harris returns from injury.

Fox is the oldest and highest-paid of those three guards. He's the obvious trade candidate, but he'll be the hardest to move. He may be a year removed from making the All-Star Game, but he's likely never making the team again if he stays on the Spurs. He's a good player, but his skills as a playmaker and shot creator are only valuable on a team that needs those abilities.

Fox is making $49.5 million this season in the first year of a four-year, $222 million contract. That is the same salary Luka Doncic is making for the Lakers , and Fox has far from Luka's impact on the floor. That deal is bad now and will continue to get worse and worse as Fox ages.

LaVine always puts up killer counting stats, but he has played on some awful teams that generally perform better when he's not on the floor. He's an efficient volume scorer, but he doesn't contribute in any other area of the game. As the league has become more about maxing out possessions via rebounding and low turnover rates, a player in LaVine's archetype has become less valuable.

DARKO has been early in understanding the importance of those areas, consistently rating LaVine as a replacement-level player. He is wildly overpaid at $49.0 million, but this could be one of the easier contracts to trade on this list simply because he does have an elite NBA skill (scoring) and he is in the last year of his contract, lowering the downside risk of any team that wanted to take a chance on him.

articles.title: Dwyane Wade drops Mavericks Cooper Flagg truth bomb
articles.summary: The Dallas Mavericks have been up and down lately, recently picking up a comfortable home win over the shorthanded Golden State Warriors. This was preceded...
articles.body:
The Dallas Mavericks have been up and down lately, recently picking up a comfortable home win over the shorthanded Golden State Warriors . This was preceded by a string of blowout losses in which reigning Rookie of the Year Cooper Flagg was largely held in check by opposing defenses.

Still, recently, NBA Hall of Famer Dwyane Wade hit Flagg with some high praise.

"You talk about a guy that has come in with expectations and has delivered on every expectation… What we all want to see in Year 2 is see that jump, especially as one of the stars in our game. We're in the midst of that jump…The future is really bright again in Dallas," said Wade, via Wy Network w/Dwyane Wade on X, formerly Twitter.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Indeed, the expectations were sky-high when Flagg was drafted number one overall by Dallas last year, especially considering that the team had inexplicably traded away its previous franchise player, Luka Doncic, just months earlier.

Flagg wasted little time establishing himself as a future star at the NBA level, and has shown some real improvements in his game in year 2, causing some to wonder if the Mavericks could sneak in as a playoff team out West with Kyrie Irving also back from injury.

There are several weak points in Flagg's game that defenses have started to notice, including a lack of a reliable jump shot, as well as shaky half-court shot creation tools outside of powering to the rim or posting up.

Still, if he stays on his current trajectory of improvement, it shouldn't be long until Flagg is able to iron out those deficiencies and take another leap forward.

articles.title: ‘Ain’t even trying to hate’ – Jeff Teague compares Tacko Fall to 3-time All-Star
articles.summary: Former NBA player Jeff Teague has compared Tacko Fall to a player who has been a defensive stalwart in the league for several years Fall was signed by the Ph...
articles.body:
Former NBA player Jeff Teague has compared Tacko Fall to a player who has been a defensive stalwart in the league for several years

Fall was signed by the Philadelphia 76ers initially on an Exhibit 10 contract, but just days later, it was converted into a two-way deal.

In the 76ers' most recent win against the Orlando Magic, Fall played 10 minutes and scored only 2 points, but he contributed defensively, recording 3 blocks.

While showcasing his highlights on the podcast, Teague made a shocking comparison between him and Rudy Gobert.

Jeff Teague speaks on Tacko Fall's journey in the NBA

Fall went undrafted in 2019 and joined the Boston Celtics after playing Summer League for them. It was during Fall's time with the Celtics that Teague shared the locker room with him and saw some glimpses of brilliance in him.

The 30-year-old spent two years in Boston and then moved to the Cleveland Cavaliers. He then played in China and other countries before making his way back into the NBA.

The Club 520 podcast crew were discussing about Fall, and how he has been playing a few valuable minutes for the team. During that conversation, Teague dropped the big statement.

"Same thing Rudy Gobert can do; he can do… I just seen Tacko catch the ball and dunk it. And I ain't even trying to hate on Rudy; I just think [Tacko Fall] never got a fair shot when he was in Boston… I used to see Tacko in practice be smooth, you know what I mean? I'm like, 'Damn, why this big m*********** don't play?'" said Teague.

Gobert is having a poor season with the Minnesota Timberwolves, as he is scoring only 7.6 points on 45.1% shooting from the field. His field goal percentage is the lowest it has ever been in his career.

This has led to a lot of criticism being directed at Gobert, with his teammates also expressing displeasure at times. However, the claim that Tacko Fall can do everything Gobert can do seems harsh, as the French player is still a four-time Defensive Player of the Year.

His form may have dipped, but Gobert is still one of the best rim protectors in the league. Fall is also a good player, but to earn a comparison with a player like Gobert, he will have to put up more consistent performances.

articles.title: UNC Basketball given bottom-half seed in latest bracketology
articles.summary: The North Carolina Tar Heels have to battle for a higher-seed in the NCAA Tournament
articles.body:
Life under Michael Malone has gotten off to a relatively decent start. While a loss against the Georgia Bulldogs and the recent injury to Neoklis Avdalas have stunted some of the offseason momentum churned by the former NBA champion, the North Carolina Tar Heels should still be involved in the Big Dance.

In Joe Lunardi's latest ESPN bracketology update , the Tar Heels were slated to be a No. 11 seed, prizing them for an opening-round matchup against fellow 11-seed Cincinnati, in the NCAA's new 76-team format.

If Malone and Co. pushed past the Bearcats, it would set them up for an enticing affair against the No. 6 Arkansas Razorbacks, setting up two of college basketball's biggest brands against one another so early in the tournament.

Over the next 13 days, UNC will be taking on a schedule that amps up, including Marshall (H), Monmouth (H), West Virginia (N), and, funnily enough, No. 20 Arkansas (H).

If the Tar Heels' debut campaign with Malone ends with an NCAA Tournament appearance of any kind, it would be North Carolina's fourth in a row. With the last tourney being missed coming in the 2022-23 calamitous season.

Despite being ranked as the nation's No. 1 team entering that season, the Hubert Davis-led squad finished with a 20-13 record, leaving them out of the field.

articles.title: Spurs guard Dylan Harper reportedly expected to miss up to 3 weeks with left rotator hip strain
articles.summary: Harper sustained the injury during San Antonio's loss to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday.
articles.body:
San Antonio Spurs guard Dylan Harper has reportedly been diagnosed with a left hip rotator strain, ESPN's Shams Charania reports .

The recovery timetable for that injury is one to three weeks, depending on how Harper's rehabilitation progresses, according to Charania.

Harper, 20, sustained the injury during the Spurs' 105-93 defeat to the Detroit Pistons on Tuesday. In the closing minute of the fourth quarter, Harper was about to receive a pass from Stephon Castle while matched up against Detroit's Ausar Thompson.

However, Harper's right foot slipped on the court and caused him to stretch awkwardly. He stayed down on the floor while play continued on the other end of the court, appearing to grab at his left hip or groin area.

The second-year guard was eventually able to stand up and walk off the court with some assistance from teammate Keldon Johnson. But he was noticeably limping and in pain as he went to the locker room. Harper did not return to the game during the final 53 seconds.

"It just looked like he slipped, obviously," Spurs coach Mitch Johnson told reporters afterward, via the San Antonio Express-News' Tom Orsborn . "So hoping for the best, but don't know anything yet."

Harper appeared at Thursday's shootaround with no noticeable limp , according to Orsborn. But that was apparently before imaging results came back from team medical staff.

"I'm happy he's not as hurt as he could be," said Spurs forward Julian Champagne, who will replace Harper in the starting lineup. "Obviously, we need him, so finding out it wasn't that serious, or as serious as it could have been, was good news."

In 15 games this season, Harper is scoring 18.4 points per game, second on San Antonio behind Victor Wembanyama. He's also averaging 5.4 rebounds and 4.5 assists. He's shooting 50% from the floor and 31% on 54 3-point attempts.

At 12-3, the Spurs are a half-game behind the Los Angeles Lakers and Philadelphia 76ers for the NBA's top record . San Antonio hosts the Los Angeles Clippers (4-9) on Thursday night, then have two days off before hosting the New Orleans Pelicans (5-11) on Saturday.
